transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. How can I help you today?

Hello, Dr. Lee. I’m stuck double‑ and triple‑checking my analyses for hours, even when I know they’re done, and it’s starting to derail my projects. It has become incredibly difficult to manage, and I'm really struggling to keep up at work.
Do you feel a strong urge to check your work repeatedly because you're afraid something bad will happen if you don't?

Yes, I feel this overwhelming urge to go back through my code, formulas, and exports for hours, even though I know it doesn't make sense to keep checking. I'm just terrified that I've made a tiny error in a dataset that could lead to the city making a really bad policy decision.
Do you find that these checking behaviors are driven by intrusive thoughts or mental images that keep coming back, even when you don't want them to?

Yes, my brain constantly latches onto these horrible "what-if" thoughts about making a tiny error that could lead to the city making a bad policy decision. Even when I know the numbers are right, I can't shut off the replay of these worst-case scenarios in my head. It feels impossible to focus on anything else until I check again to be absolutely certain.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidate was [F42], and based on the patient's description of recurrent intrusive thoughts (e.g., 'what-if' fears about making an error leading to bad policy decisions) and compulsive checking behaviors performed to reduce anxiety, this remains consistent with the diagnostic criteria for F42 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder). The symptoms are ego-dystonic, time-consuming, and significantly impairing occupational functioning, which further supports maintaining F42 as the sole candidate. No new symptoms suggesting alternative diagnoses (e.g., mood disorders, psychosis, or anxiety disorders with different phenomenology) have emerged.
